readout_other: tungsten microelectrode recording; fiber photometry of jGCaMP8m calcium signal; comparison with flash light stimulation of the eye
direction_notes: US to the visual cortex evoked neuronal spiking and calcium responses with shorter latency than flash light stimulation; longer US evoked longer responses.

exposures.label: 3.6 MHz ring transducer to rat visual cortex, 30 ms and 60 ms stimulation

timing.protocol_description: 3.6 MHz sine wave in burst mode, stimulation time 30 ms (cycle = 107 k) and 60 ms (cycle = 214 k), interval 5 s; the methods also mention a '250 ms Burst cycle' for the field measurements. Light stimulation (flash <1 ms) delivered for comparison.

source_quotes.n_subjects: Long-Evans (LE) rats (n = 10) were used for this study.
source_quotes.exposures[0].fundamental_frequency_khz: A 3.6 MHz ring transducer with a focal depth of 23 mm was used for this experiment.
source_quotes.exposures[0].free_field.pressure_kpa: The peak-to-peak amplitude of the focused ultrasound pressure, as measured in the free field, was 3.6 MPa

flags.reason: Peak-to-peak 3.6 MPa (MI 2.6) in free field; skull transmission 0.5-0.6 and MI 1.3-1.6 through skull given but no in situ pressure value.
Source text is garbled by overlapping OCR; 30 ms and 60 ms single bursts per trial, treated as continuous. '250 ms Burst cycle' in field-measurement methods not reconciled.
No transducer maker or builder named ('PZT ring transducer').
Only control is transducer and electrodes placed in water to check for electrical and vibration artefact; no sham US arm in vivo.
Authors argue against auditory route from latency and V1-restricted GCaMP expression; no control experiment or masking.
Methods describe a cranial window over the visual cortex while results say non-invasive through the skull; skull-in-path hydrophone measurements were made.
